clips.spoken: Practice eight. Daniel has a meeting in ten minutes, but his slides are not ready. Choose all the reasonable recommendations. We are checking usefulness.
Let us build advice. We need three pieces.
Exit check, part three. Your friend has too many emails and feels stressed. Give your own recommendation, and explain why.
The trip improved a little, but other problems are still open. Another step might help.
Meet Maya. Tomorrow morning, she has an important presentation.
Tonight, she has three small problems.
First, her outline is not finished.
Second, her phone keeps buzzing with notifications.
Third, she is not sure where the meeting will be.
These problems are manageable. But Maya feels stuck.
Hmm. What should I do?
This question is the key to our class. When we need help, we ask: What should I do?
Now take a moment. Tell a partner about a small problem you have this week.
Thank you. In this class, you will practice natural English for exactly this.
Problem one. Maya has not finished her outline. What can she do? Think for a moment.
Here are some ideas. Which one would you try first?
Problem two. Her phone keeps buzzing. It is hard to focus. What can Maya do?
Here are some ideas. Which one is realistic for you?
Problem three. Maya is not sure where the meeting will be. What can she do?
Here are some ideas. Do you have another one?
Today you will learn three things.
First, you can ask for advice.
Second, you can give a useful recommendation.
Third, you can explain a reason.
Now watch Maya and her coworker Daniel.
What should I do?
I think you should finish the outline first, because it is the biggest problem.
That is a good idea. Thanks for the advice.
Ask. Recommend. Explain why. Let us begin.
Turn to a partner. Say the three goals: ask, recommend, explain.
Well done.
Scene one. A coworking space. Daniel has six tasks, and only one afternoon.
He feels overwhelmed. He asks his coworker Priya for help.
I have so many tasks! What should I do?
What could Priya say? Think of one idea.
I think you should start with the most urgent task.
Watch the action. Daniel finds the urgent task and puts it first.
Why does this advice fit? Daniel has too many choices. Priya recommends one clear, useful next step.
That is a good idea. Thanks for the advice.
Now your turn. What else could Priya recommend?
For example: You should ask a coworker to help with one task. Or: You should make a short list. Many ideas can work.
Repeat after me: You should start with the most urgent task.
Good. Now tell your partner a problem, and give one recommendation.
Thank you.
Scene two. A train station. Priya has an early train tomorrow, and she does not want to be late.
My train leaves early tomorrow. What should I do?
Her friend Marcus sees two paths. Look at the paths. Which path is more useful?
Think about the road, the weather, and the time.
I think you should leave an hour earlier. The road may be busy.
The useful path becomes clear. The other path fades.
Why does this fit? Priya wants to avoid stress. A little extra time is a simple, useful action.
But notice: the result is only possible. Maybe the road is quiet. Maybe not. Advice gives a good next step, not a promise.
Good idea. Thanks for the advice.
Your turn. Give Priya another reason to leave earlier.
For example: because the station may be crowded.
Share your reason with a partner.
Scene three. An apartment. Hana has early meetings. Her roommate Theo practices music late at night.
The music is loud at night, and I start work early. What should I do?
Her friend Marcus is visiting. Should she say nothing? Should she be angry? Think about a polite option.
I think you should talk to him calmly. Tell him what you need.
Watch the action. Hana talks with Theo, and the music changes.
Oh, sorry! I can use headphones after ten.
Why does this fit? A calm talk respects both people. It gives Theo a chance to help.
Again, there is no guarantee. Theo might forget tomorrow. Advice is a useful next step, and context matters.
Your turn. What else can Hana say to Theo? Share one polite sentence with a partner.
Good. Polite advice helps people listen.
Let us compare advice with a rule.
You must wear a badge in this building.
This is a rule. There is no choice.
You should arrive early tomorrow.
This is advice. It is a useful idea, and you can think about it.
Context also changes how strong advice sounds. The same sentence from a close friend feels gentle. From a manager, it can feel stronger.
So listen to the person, the place, and the situation.
Quick check. Is each sentence a rule, or is it advice?
A problem can have more than one good answer. Daniel will be late for a meeting.
Three ideas are reasonable. One idea is not useful.
Good advice depends on the person, the place, and the time.
Your turn. Give a fifth idea. Start with: You should.
One more thing. Look at this sentence.
The train should arrive soon.
Here, should means we expect something. Nobody is giving advice. It is not the meaning we study today.
In this class, should means a useful recommendation.
Which sentence gives advice?
First, a subject. Who is the advice for? You, she, we, they.
Second, the advice word: should.
Third, the base verb. This is the simple verb: check, call, ask, save.
Add the rest of the idea, and you have advice.
Subject, plus should, plus base verb.
Say it with me: You should check the address.
Your turn. Make your own sentence: a subject, should, and a base verb.
For example: We should leave earlier. Share it with a partner.
Now watch the word should. Change the subject, and look.
I should call.
You should call.
He should call.
She should call.
We should call.
They should call.
Should stays the same. The verb stays the same too. No s, no ending.
Tap a subject and try it yourself.
Say each sentence aloud with a partner. Change the subject each time.
Many learners add extra words. Let us remove them.
First, no s. After should, use the base verb. Not calls.
Second, no to. After should, do not say to.
Third, no does or doesn't. Should already works as the helper. The negative is shouldn't.
So remember four things. Base verb. No s. No to. No do, does, or did.
Your turn. Fix this sentence aloud: She should goes home.
The answer: She should go home. Base verb, no s.
The verb be also works. Keep be after should.
You should be on time.
Not: you should are. Not: you should is. Just be.
You shouldn't be rude.
Good advice can be positive or negative.
Your turn. Make a sentence with be. What should a good coworker be?
Match each advice sentence to the best situation. Tap an advice sentence, then tap a scene.
Daniel has an important file open. His laptop battery is low.
You should save your work.
That is positive advice. Save is a useful action.
And you shouldn't close the file yet.
That is negative advice. It recommends against one action. Closing the file now is not a helpful path.
The full form is should not. The short form is shouldn't. Both are correct. In speech, we usually say shouldn't.
Shouldn't is not a strict rule like mustn't. It means: this is not a good idea.
Your turn. Tell a partner one thing you should do, and one thing you shouldn't do, before an important meeting.
Build each sentence. Tap the words in order. Watch for extra words.
Do not make a negative just by adding n't. Ask: does it make sense?
If the address might be wrong, you should check it. You shouldn't check it? That does not help.
But if a message from your manager arrives, you shouldn't ignore it. That makes sense.
Choose the action first. Then decide: is it useful, or is it not useful?
Your turn. Say one meaningful negative sentence.
Now we ask for advice. Priya's sister is waiting for an answer, and Priya is not sure what to do.
Look at the statement: I should call her.
To make a direct question, move should in front of the subject.
Should, then the subject, then the base verb. No do. No does. No did.
Should I call her?
That is a natural question. Listen for should at the start.
Your turn. Ask me a question with should. For example: Should I send the email?
We can add a question word at the start: what, when, who, or where.
Question word, plus should, plus subject, plus base verb.
A useful question when you do not know the next step.
When should we leave?
This asks about time.
Who should I ask?
This asks about a person. Where should we meet? This asks about a place.
Pair practice. Ask your partner a question with what, when, or who.
A café. Hana is giving a short talk on Monday. She asks Marcus for advice.
I am giving a short talk on Monday. What should I do?
What would Marcus say? Think.
Have you practiced out loud?
Not yet. Should I practice with my slides?
Yes, you should. And you should time yourself.
When should I start?
I think you should start tonight. Then you can change things tomorrow.
That is a good idea. Thanks for the advice.
Notice the turns: a question, a short answer, a reason. Tap any line to hear it again.
Now role-play the first three lines with a partner.
Short answers repeat should. The pronoun matches the speaker.
Yes, you should.
I changes to you. And do not forget the comma. Or the negative:
No, you shouldn't.
Should we leave now?
Yes, we should.
We stays we. A helpful answer can add a reason or an alternative:
No, you shouldn't. You should check first.
Short answer, then reason. That is helpful advice.
Pair practice. Ask, answer, and add a reason.
Listen to the word should. The letter l is silent.
should
In a strong form, it sounds like this. Use it when you stress the word, or when it comes at the end.
Yes, you should.
In connected speech, the word is often shorter and weaker.
PH:juː ʃəd kˈɔːl hɜː.
You do not have to use the weak form every time. The strong form is always clear and correct.
shouldn't
Shouldn't has two syllables. The last t is very light.
Now you try. Say should, strong. Then say: You should call her.
Listen and repeat. First at natural speed, then slowly.
You should call her.
You should call her.
Should I call her?
Should I call her?
What should I do?
What should I do?
You shouldn't ignore the message.
You shouldn't ignore the message.
You can soften advice with: I think you should.
I think you should ask for help.
To recommend against something, say: I don't think you should.
I don't think you should send it yet.
You can also say: You shouldn't send it yet. Both are natural. The I don't think form often sounds softer.
How can you respond? You can accept the advice, or you can say you are not sure.
That is a good idea.
Thanks for the advice.
I am not sure that will work.
Pair practice. Give advice with I think you should, and respond.
Practice one. Match each advice to its problem. We are checking meaning.
Practice two. Build the sentence. Some tiles are traps. We are checking grammar.
Practice three. Read the situation. Choose should or shouldn't.
Practice four. These sentences are incorrect. Find the mistake and repair it. We are checking grammar.
Practice five. Build the question. Remember: should goes before the subject.
Practice six. Choose the short answer that matches the question.
Practice seven. Add a useful reason. A reason starts with because.
Two different questions. Is the sentence grammatical? And is the advice useful in this situation?
You should ignore the meeting: the grammar is correct, but the advice is not helpful.
You should to call her: the idea may be fine, but the grammar needs repair.
Scenario one. The big presentation. Maya presents tomorrow morning.
Problem one: the outline is not finished. Problem two: the phone keeps buzzing. Problem three: she is not sure about the room.
Which problem would you solve first?
Scenario two. A group trip. Priya, Marcus, and Hana want to take an early train on Saturday.
Problem one: nobody has bought the tickets. Problem two: the train leaves very early. Problem three: the friends live far apart.
Scenario three. A shared apartment. Hana has early meetings. Her roommate Theo practices music in the evening.
Problem one: the music is loud late at night. Problem two: Hana needs sleep before work. Problem three: they have no clear agreement.
Choose the problem to solve first in each scenario. There is no single correct answer. Be ready to explain why.
Round one. Maya's presentation. Partner A, you are Maya: ask for advice. Partner B, you are the advisor: give a recommendation and a reason. Then choose the path your pair picked.
Maya finishes the outline. She feels calmer, but the phone still buzzes, and the room is still a question.
The phone is quiet. Maya can think clearly, but the outline still needs work, and the room is still a question.
Maya checks the invitation and finds the building. She knows where to go, but the outline is still unfinished.
Round two. The group trip. Switch roles. Partner B asks for advice. Partner A gives a recommendation and a reason. Then choose the path your pair picked.
The tickets are bought. Everyone can board, but the meeting time and the plan are still unclear.
The friends agree to arrive early. There is time to adapt, but the tickets are still not bought.
The group message shows the plan. Everyone knows the meeting point, but the tickets are still not bought.
Round three. The shared apartment. Switch roles again. Partner A asks for advice. Partner B gives a recommendation and a reason. Then choose the path your pair picked.
Hana talks with Theo calmly. He listens, and they understand each other better, though they have no agreement yet.
Hana leaves a friendly note. Theo reads it, but he cannot answer right away, so the situation stays unclear.
Hana wears headphones and sleeps better tonight. The problem is not discussed, so it might return tomorrow.
New information! The manager moved the meeting thirty minutes earlier, and the room has changed.
Does your advice still work? Listen to Maya's needs, and revise your recommendation.
Daniel checks the room for her. That might save time, and Maya can keep working.
Maya shortens the presentation. The outline is ready, and the shorter version fits the new time.
Maya turns off her phone and works faster. She is focused, though other questions remain.
Your two steps work together. Maya feels prepared. Nothing is guaranteed, but she has a clear plan.
Maya improved something, but other problems are still open. Another step might help.
New information! The train is delayed by forty minutes, and Marcus is still at home.
Does your advice still work? Listen to the group's needs, and revise your recommendation.
Hana sends a message. Marcus sees it and leaves a little later. That might reduce stress for everyone.
Priya and Hana wait at a café near the station. The delay feels shorter, though Marcus still needs to know.
Priya checks the app and finds a later train. It helps, but the group still needs one clear plan.
Your two steps cover different problems. The group has a clearer plan for the delay. Delays can still surprise us, so stay flexible.
New information! Theo has a concert on Saturday. He needs to practice every evening this week.
Does your advice still work? Listen to both people's needs, and revise your recommendation.
They agree: music until ten, and headphones after that. Both people have a plan.
Over coffee, Theo explains the concert, and Hana explains her mornings. They understand each other better.
Theo practices earlier in the evening. Hana can rest, though they still need a clear agreement.
Your steps cover different needs. Hana and Theo can work out a clearer plan. It still depends on both people, so keep talking.
Some things improved, but at least one need is still open. Another step might help.
Share your recommendations with another pair. Which path did you choose? What was your reason? Compare your ideas, and listen for different good answers.
Look at what happened. Each choice changed the situation, and new information changed it again.
Good advisers listen to the person's needs. They give a reason. And they revise their advice when the facts change.
Notice also: no path was a guarantee. Advice helps, but the result can still be uncertain.
Now let us bring our ideas together.
Turn to a partner. What new information changed your advice? Say it in one sentence.
Let us connect everything.
Advice is a recommendation. It is a useful idea, not a guarantee, and not automatically a rule.
For affirmative advice: subject, should, base verb.
For negative advice: subject, shouldn't, base verb. It recommends against an action.
In a direct question, the modal moves before the subject. No do, no does, no did.
Short answers match the speaker and the subject: Yes, you should. No, we shouldn't.
And helpful advice considers the person's situation, and often includes a reason.
Ask. Recommend. Explain why.
Choose one box. Say a new example sentence for it.
Feedback time. Think about the roleplays. Teacher, share one good example you heard, and one thing to improve. Use the checklist if it helps.
Exit check, part one. This sentence is incorrect. Choose the repair.
Exit check, part two. Ask for advice in a new situation. Say it aloud or type it in chat. Many questions are possible.
Here is the feedback. Part one has one correct repair. Parts two and three can have many good answers. Check form, and check usefulness.
Well done. You can ask for advice, give a recommendation, and explain why.
Say one sentence you will use this week.
